balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For Lloyds Banking Group plc: equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For Lloyds Banking Group plc: the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For Lloyds Banking Group plc: the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For Lloyds Banking Group plc: the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For Lloyds Banking Group plc: the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For Lloyds Banking Group plc: CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For Lloyds Banking Group plc: the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

nii.title: Net interest income
nii.content:
Net interest income (NII) is interest earned on loans and other assets less interest paid on deposits and wholesale funding -- the core spread of a deposit-funded lender.

For Lloyds Banking Group plc: NII is the majority of total income and is driven less by loan growth than by the structural hedge, which converts low/non-interest-bearing current-account balances into duration-matched income (~£5.5bn FY2025, guided to ~£7bn FY2026 and ~£8bn FY2027 as low-yielding hedge tranches roll into current market rates).

What to watch:

  • NIM direction (3.06% FY2025, 3.19% H1 2026) versus the pace of Bank of England rate cuts
  • Whether structural hedge income is offsetting mortgage back-book refinancing at the guided pace

depositsFunding.title: Deposits and wholesale funding
depositsFunding.content:
Customer deposits are the low-cost current-account and savings balances that fund the loan book; debt securities in issue is wholesale/MREL funding raised in capital markets to fill the gap and meet regulatory requirements.

For Lloyds Banking Group plc: Lloyds is the UK's largest current-account and savings franchise, so the deposit base (not wholesale funding) is the moat; a rising reliance on debt securities would signal deposit attrition to challenger banks (Monzo, Starling, Chase UK) or to higher-yielding savings products.

What to watch:

  • Deposit growth relative to debt securities in issue (log scale shows the gap)
  • Mix shift from non-interest-bearing current accounts into priced savings, which erodes the structural hedge benefit

costOfRisk.title: Cost base and credit impairment
costOfRisk.content:
Operating expenses are the bank's cost base (staff, technology, remediation); credit impairment charge is the expected-loss provision taken against the loan book. The line shows impairment as a share of net interest income -- a rough cost-of-risk relative to the spread it is charged against.

For Lloyds Banking Group plc: the impairment charge rose from £431m (FY2024) to £795m (FY2025) as UK consumer/commercial credit quality normalized off post-pandemic lows; Accelerate 2030 targets a cost-income ratio below 45% by 2030 via ~£2bn of further AI/technology-driven savings, on top of operating expenses that already carry recurring conduct/remediation costs (motor finance).

What to watch:

  • Impairment charge accelerating faster than NII growth -- a UK recession or unemployment shock would hit the unsecured, credit card and SME books first
  • Operating expenses excluding one-off remediation/redress charges, to see the underlying cost-income trend Accelerate 2030 is targeting

statutoryVsOrdinary.title: Statutory profit vs ordinary shareholders' net income
statutoryVsOrdinary.content:
Profit for the period is the Group's total statutory profit after tax, before deducting coupons on preference shares, AT1/other equity instruments and non-controlling interests. Net income is what is left for ordinary shareholders and is the basis for EPS.

For Lloyds Banking Group plc: the gap includes AT1 coupon payments that are a cash cost of the capital stack but not a line item ordinary shareholders see in EPS; FY2025's statutory profit after tax of £4,757m already carried an £800m motor finance redress charge (underlying profit after tax excluding it was £5,428m), so both lines understate run-rate earnings power in FY2025-H1 2026.

What to watch:

  • A widening gap signalling a growing AT1/preference coupon burden as capital stack mix shifts
  • One-off conduct/redress charges (motor finance) distorting the statutory line versus management's "underlying" profit framing

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For Lloyds Banking Group plc: the growth rate matters more than the level; compare it with the DCF's base-case growth path below.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For Lloyds Banking Group plc: the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue
